title: A handful of beans
hookLine: food shrinks to almost nothing; his spine shows through his belly like a string of beads (MN 36)

cards: There's a stone statue in the Lahore Museum, in Pakistan, from the old region of Gandhara. A man sits cross-legged in meditation. His face is calm.
But his body is barely a body. Every rib stands out. The veins run like cords over his arms.

His belly has sunk back almost to his spine. It's called the Fasting Buddha, and it shows the wanderer as he would later describe himself, in the forest near Uruvela. Forcing the breath hadn't worked.
So he turned to another ascetic method. Eat less. Then less.

teach.b: Again, the Buddha tells it himself, and he doesn't spare the details. He cut his food to a handful at a time: a little bean soup, lentils, peas. His body wasted away.
His limbs became like the knotted joints of vine stems, his backside like a camel's hoof. His ribs stuck out like the rafters of an old, broken shed.
The gleam of his eyes sank deep into their sockets, like the gleam of water at the bottom of a deep well. His scalp shriveled like a green gourd left in the sun.

teach.h: A SPINE LIKE A STRING OF BEADS.
teach.b: When he touched his belly, he could feel his spine, pressing through like a string of beads. When he rubbed his limbs, the hair fell out at the roots. Some who saw him said he was black, others said brown.
His clear, bright skin had lost its color. Then comes the line that turns the story.
By this painful practice, he says, I did not reach anything beyond ordinary human states. No special knowledge. No freedom.
Just starvation. Why so much detail? Because some ascetics of his time held that the more you denied the body, the closer you came to truth.
He had tried it, and he reports back plainly: it didn't work.
In this story, the body isn't the enemy.

how: Theravada monks and nuns eat their meals before noon under the monastic rule, eating enough to sustain practice rather than starving, and the Fasting Buddha image recalls the path the Buddha tried and set aside.

o: the hard austerities he tried: doing what is hard to do
the bowl of food a monk carries on alms rounds
a holy fast kept once a year to purify the body

games.q: what's inside the fasting — tap the pairs.
p: like rafters of an old shed
like water deep in a well
a statue in the Lahore Museum

s: the Buddha taught that fasting to the bone brings wisdom
he tried it and said it brought nothing beyond ordinary human states.
the Buddha describes his starving body in detail himself
in MN 36: vine joints, a camel's hoof, a string of beads.
the Fasting Buddha statue is in the Lahore Museum
a stone carving from the old region of Gandhara.

games.q: you've cut your food to a handful of bean soup at a time. your spine shows through your belly. has it brought freedom?
o: not yet, so eat even less.
no: nothing beyond ordinary human states.
games.why: he says it plainly: by this painful practice he reached nothing beyond the ordinary. starving isn't holy.

practice: Picture your next meal, or if you have something to eat nearby, take one small bite and chew it much more slowly than usual: the taste arriving, the texture, the way the body leans toward it.
Think of the hands that grew it, carried it and cooked it, and as you swallow, let being fed be a kindness, not a guilt. Then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Dukkarakarika. The hard austerities of the wanderer's fasting, down to a handful of beans, and the proof, in his own words, that starving the body doesn't free the mind.

orig.note: Pali: the doing of what is hard to do, the name for the Bodhisatta's austerities.

carryVoice: Your line: starving isn't holy. Your body is a friend you're feeding. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the fasting and its similes
